title: The scholar's mistake
hook: a person can recite the driving manual and still run the red light: the Patti says reading without living the letters is still not learning

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letters of the mind: kakai, dadai and tatai, school letters turned into lessons for the soul. Your line was the soul's lessons. When something went wrong, did you try dadai first? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

A driving test comes in two parts. One happens at a desk, with a pencil. The other happens at a real crossing, with a real car coming. Someone can pass the first and fail the second, and only the second keeps anyone safe on the road. The Patti has a sharp line about which one counts. It's hidden in the second half of its center line, the half we held back yesterday. Today: the scholar's mistake.
screen: `THE MANUAL, AND THE RED LIGHT.` → `KNOWING AND LIVING.` → `WHICH ONE COUNTS?`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Rahao spoke to the mind: why do you forget, foolish mind? Here's how it finishes, in paraphrase: when you give your account, brother, then you'll be counted as educated. The word for educated is parhiaa: one who has read. So the Patti redefines the word for a reader. You haven't really read until you can give an account of your life. Not of the book. Of your life. That's the scholar's mistake: thinking the reading is the finish line. Second, the letter ngangai says it straight out. In paraphrase: whoever understands true wisdom, that one is the learned pandit. And the next line shows what that understanding looks like: one who knows the One in all beings doesn't go around saying I, I. So the proof of learning isn't how much you can recite. It's whether you can see the One in the person in front of you, and let go of your own self-importance. Third, this isn't a poem against study. Guru Nanak put deep teaching on a schoolboard. The Patti honors the letters. It just won't let them stay on the board. Fourth, think about the kind of account the Rahao means. Not a test score. A life story with the deeds left in. Did the letter dadai make you blame less? Did tatai make you put on less of a show? Did sasai make you see one Master over everyone? That's the exam. A person who has never read a word could pass it. A person who has read everything could fail. Today's line: live the letters.
screen: `PARHIAA: ONE WHO HAS READ.` · `NGANGAI: WISDOM MAKES THE PANDIT.` · `NOT AGAINST STUDY.` · `THE ACCOUNT IS A LIFE.` · then, large: `LIVE THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one word to live today. Settle, and breathe. From the Patti's letters, pick one: made, from sasai; blame no one, from dadai; or no show, from tatai. Say it once in your head. Now think of one real moment in the hours ahead where that word could show up: a meeting, a phone call, a line at the store. See yourself there, living the word instead of just knowing it. Then let the picture go and rest with the breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.

The scholar's mistake. Thinking reading is the finish line. The Patti says you're counted educated when you can give the account of your life, and the pandit is the one who sees the One in all. Today's word.
Your line: live the letters. Take the one word you chose and do it once today where someone can see it, then let that be your whole lesson. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikh teaching pairs study of Gurbani with living it, often summed up as reading the Guru's word and then practicing it in daily conduct, seva and honest work.

original.note: parhiaa: one who has read, the educated one; the Patti says you are this when you give your account.

trapdoor: what you thought: the scholar's mistake is a wrong fact.
what it means: it's thinking reading is the finish line; the Patti says the account of a life is the real test.
what a scholar hears: parhiaa, one who has read, is redefined in the Rahao, and ngangai makes the pandit the one who sees the One in all and drops the I.
